summary: A 1975 Telnet option to transmit a special extended ASCII used at the Stanford and MIT artificial intelligence labs. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 5198.

plainLanguage.summary: The Telnet EXTEND-ASCII option allows peers to send characters using two 8-bit bytes, including extra bits that some programs treat specially. The option is off by default, and RFC 698 was later replaced by RFC 5198.

subtitle: A Telnet option for sending characters with additional control bits

tldr.problem: Some sites used characters with extra control bits that ordinary Telnet text could not represent as intended.
tldr.mechanism: The EXTEND-ASCII option lets peers negotiate transmission of a character as two 8-bit bytes.
tldr.outcome: The option defaults to standard NVT ASCII and RFC 698 was later obsoleted by RFC 5198.

sections.title: Characters Beyond Standard NVT ASCII
sections.content:
Some sites, including Stanford AI and MIT AI, used keyboards that treated almost all 128 characters as printable and used additional bits as control bits. Programs used those bits as command modifiers or to separate textual input from command input.

Without the additional bits, some characters could be interpreted as control characters. The RFC gives the Greek letter beta and CONTROL-C as an example of a conflict on a Telnet connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Some programs needed extra character information to distinguish text from commands. This option provides a way to transmit that information over Telnet.

sections.title: Encoding an Extended Character
sections.content:
The EXTEND-ASCII option has Telnet option code 17. Its subcommand carries an extended character as two consecutive 8-bit bytes: first the high-order bits, then the low-order bits.

At Stanford AI and MIT AI, bit 8 is the CONTROL bit and bit 9 is the META bit. The exact meaning of additional bits depends on the user program; the particular Stanford character set shown in the RFC is for reference and is not required by the option.
sections.plainLanguage: The option sends a character in two bytes, with the higher bits first. Programs at the named labs used two extra bits called CONTROL and META.

sections.title: Negotiation and Default
sections.content:
The option uses Telnet WILL, WON'T, DO and DON'T commands to request, permit or stop extended ASCII transmission. Its default is DON'T and WON'T, which means the connection uses standard NVT ASCII unless the peers negotiate otherwise.

The RFC says that ordinary 7-bit ASCII is used most of the time, with extended ASCII expected to be sent as an escape-character sequence when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must negotiate before sending extended characters. Until then, they use standard NVT ASCII.
